description:
Solo builder of "Flame in Freefall", an AI-powered dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research searchable for fire safety insights.

About me: JEE aspirant focused on AI engineering, comfortable across the stack (data pipelines, backend, LLMs/RAG). I'm also an author, so I care about making technical stuff readable.
summary: Cosmic Fire is an AI-powered fire-safety explorer built from real NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data. Fire behaves very differently in microgravity, and a crew can't simply walk away from one, so understanding how materials burn and how smoke behaves is critical for spacecraft safety. The data arrived as dozens of mixed files (PDFs, Excel, CSV, Word, PowerPoint, text), so I built a pipeline that sorts them by type: tables become interactive charts, and documents are split into searchable chunks. The dashboard compares solid-fuel burn tests (BASS-II), smoke tests (SAME-R), and spacecraft-scale fire tests (SAFFIRE-II). Anyone can ask the research reports questions in plain language and get cited answers from Google Gemini, and an "Explain" button turns computed statistics into fire-safety insights. It makes dense NASA research easier for students and the public to explore.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Cosmic Fire lets a user explore microgravity combustion and smoke experiments from NASA PSI in two ways: (1) interactive charts built from experiment tables, and (2) a question box that answers from the investigations' own reports, with the source files shown.

HOW IT WORKS

- Text pipeline: PDFs, Word, PowerPoint and text files are converted to text, split into chunks, and tagged by investigation. A keyword (TF-IDF) search finds the most relevant chunks for a question, and Google Gemini writes a plain-language answer that cites its sources. It is instructed to answer only from the retrieved excerpts.

- Table pipeline: the experiment tables for BASS-II (solid fuel burning), SAME-R (smoke) and SAFFIRE-II (spacecraft-scale fires) are cleaned in pandas and plotted with Plotly. The "Explain what the data shows" button sends Python-computed summary statistics (not raw data) to Gemini, which is instructed not to do its own arithmetic or interpret columns it can't verify.

- Data used: NASA PSI investigations BASS-II, SAME-R, SAFFIRE-II and ACME (ACME as a document source).

TOOLS

Python, pandas, Plotly, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Google Gemini API, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud.

USE OF AI

Code was written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). Answers and chart explanations in the app are generated at runtime by Google Gemini from NASA PSI text and tables. No images, video or audio were AI-generated, and no NASA logos or branding are used.

LIMITATIONS

The charts use each investigation's summary experiment table, not the raw sensor data. Test counts per material are small, so findings are observations rather than proof. Retrieval is keyword-based and sometimes surfaces weak matches, which could be improved with embeddings.

IMPACT

Dense technical reports are hard for students and the public to read. This tool lets someone ask a question about spacecraft fire safety and see where the answer comes from, and it shows how to handle a messy mix of file types for any future dataset.

LINKS

Live website: https://cosmicfire.streamlit.app/

Code: https://github.com/Venky0608/Cosmic-Fire
